[RESPONSE] I’ve been feeling increasingly fatigued for about six months, and during that time, I’ve lost about 5 kilograms without trying — I haven’t changed my diet or activity level, and I still have a good appetite.

[THOUGHT] Unintentional weight loss (>5% body weight over 6–12 months) plus persistent fatigue raises concern for systemic illness. Key categories include endocrine (e.g., hyperthyroidism, diabetes), malignancy, chronic infection (e.g., TB, HIV), or inflammatory conditions. Given preserved appetite, malabsorption is less likely; malignancy and hyperthyroidism remain high on the differential. Next, I should screen for classic systemic symptoms — fever, night sweats, bowel changes, cough, palpitations, heat intolerance — to narrow possibilities. Fever/night sweats suggest infection or lymphoma; palpitations/heat intolerance point to hyperthyroidism.

[QUERY] Have you experienced any of the following: fever, drenching night sweats, new or worsening cough, palpitations (racing or pounding heart), heat intolerance (feeling unusually hot), or changes in bowel habits (like diarrhea or constipation)?

13. Denies night sweats.  
14. Denies changes in bowel or bladder habits.  
[RESPONSE] I have not had fever, night sweats, or any changes in my bowel habits.

[THOUGHT] Absence of fever, night sweats, and bowel changes makes chronic infection (e.g., TB, HIV), lymphoma, and IBD less likely — though not excluded. No cough reduces suspicion for pulmonary malignancy or TB. The preserved appetite and weight loss + fatigue + possible palpitations/heat intolerance (not yet confirmed) still strongly suggest hyperthyroidism. Palpitations and heat intolerance are hallmark symptoms — I must confirm their presence. Also, unintentional weight loss with fatigue warrants checking for diabetes (polyuria/polydipsia), but patient hasn’t mentioned thirst or urination changes yet — that’s a secondary priority.

[QUERY] Have you noticed your heart racing or pounding (especially at rest), feeling unusually warm or sweating more than usual, or increased thirst or urination?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing my heart racing or pounding at rest, feeling unusually warm, sweating more than usual, or having increased thirst or urination.

[THOUGHT] The absence of classic hyperthyroid symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, sweating) and diabetic symptoms (polydipsia, polyuria) makes those diagnoses less likely — though subclinical or atypical presentations remain possible. Unintentional weight loss + fatigue without systemic B symptoms (fever/night sweats) or GI symptoms narrows the differential toward malignancy (e.g., lymphoma, gastric, pancreatic, lung), chronic infection (e.g., latent TB, HIV), or less common endocrine causes (e.g., adrenal insufficiency, pheochromocytoma — though latter usually has hypertension/palpitations). Next, I should assess for lymphadenopathy, skin changes, or respiratory symptoms not yet covered — but since cough was already denied, focus shifts to physical signs that may be reported (e.g., lumps, swelling, easy bruising, bone pain) and risk factors (e.g., smoking, family history of cancer, travel, HIV risk). Also, age is critical: weight loss in older adults raises malignancy concern more strongly. I need to ask about age and key risk factors.

I don’t smoke, and I haven’t been exposed to anyone with tuberculosis. As for family history, I don’t recall any details about cancer, autoimmune disease, or chronic infections in my family.

[THOUGHT] At age 72, unintentional weight loss and fatigue significantly increase concern for occult malignancy — especially gastrointestinal (e.g., gastric, colorectal, pancreatic) or hematologic (e.g., lymphoma, myeloma). Absence of smoking reduces (but doesn’t eliminate) lung cancer risk. No TB exposure lowers infectious risk. Given the absence of B symptoms, GI symptoms, or endocrine clues so far, next highest-yield step is to assess for subtle GI red flags: early satiety, dysphagia, melena, hematochezia, or jaundice — which may suggest upper/lower GI malignancy or hepatobiliary disease. Also, easy bruising or bone pain could hint at myeloma or metastatic disease. These are low-risk, high-specificity questions that can further stratify risk.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any difficulty swallowing, feeling full quickly after eating small amounts, dark or tarry stools, rectal bleeding, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or unexplained bruising or bone pain?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing any of those symptoms — no trouble swallowing, no feeling full quickly, no dark or tarry stools, no rectal bleeding, no yellowing of my skin or eyes, and no unexplained bruising or bone pain.

[THOUGHT] The patient is 72 years old with 6 months of unintentional weight loss (5 kg) and fatigue, no B symptoms, no GI red flags, no endocrine or infectious clues, and no obvious risk factors. This remains highly concerning for occult malignancy — particularly gastrointestinal or hematologic — but clinical evaluation alone is insufficient to rule it out. Next step must be objective testing: a complete blood count (CBC) to screen for anemia (e.g., from GI bleeding or myeloma), leukocytosis/lymphocytosis (lymphoproliferative disorder), or cytopenias; and basic metabolic panel (BMP) and liver enzymes to assess for renal/hepatic dysfunction or electrolyte imbalances. Additionally, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is still warranted to definitively exclude subclinical or atypical hyperthyroidism — even without classic symptoms — given its high prevalence in older adults and potential for apathetic presentation.

[TEST] Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, basic metabolic panel (BMP), liver function tests (LFTs), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

1. WBC: 16,000 /μL (elevated).  
2. Hemoglobin: 11 g/dL (low).  
3. Platelets: Normal.  
4. Direct Antiglobulin Test: Positive.  
5. Peripheral blood smear: Increased lymphocytes with smudge cells.  

Not specified  
Not specified  
Not specified

[THOUGHT] The lab results are highly suggestive of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL): elevated WBC with lymphocytosis, smudge cells on peripheral smear (pathognomonic), and positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) — which occurs in ~25% of CLL cases and can cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), explaining the anemia (Hb 11 g/dL). Fatigue and unintentional weight loss are common systemic symptoms in CLL, especially with AIHA or advanced disease. Age (72) aligns perfectly with typical CLL onset (median ~70 years). No other malignancy or infection explains this constellation as cohesively. While flow cytometry is confirmatory, the triad of lymphocytosis + smudge cells + DAT+ in an older adult with B-symptom–like presentation makes CLL the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
